summary: This submission conducts a systematic differential test across three major Citation File Format (CFF) converters (ruby-cff, cffconvert, and citation-js) using 38 targeted synthetic test cases. The benchmark exposes significant semantic divergences and downstream BibTeX formatting hazards, particularly regarding preferred-citation handling, DOI/URL precedence, and character escaping. The paper is well-written and factually accurate, though the lack of an accompanying code repository limits full push-button reproducibility.
strengths: Applies differential testing rigorously to an important yet overlooked aspect of scholarly software citation infrastructure.
Carefully isolates variables across 38 schema-valid edge cases spanning names, DOIs, URLs, version formats, and preferred citations.
Uncovers concrete downstream hazards that silently corrupt BibTeX and LaTeX parsing, such as unescaped special characters and unbraced entity names.
Factual claims, upstream bug reports, and converter design choices are accurately grounded in official project documentation and issue trackers.
weaknesses: No supporting repository was provided with the submission, preventing exact push-button replication of the 38 test files and harness.
Relies entirely on synthetic micro-benchmarks without validating the frequency of these edge cases across a corpus of real-world repositories.
Excludes other conversion targets supported by the tools, such as RIS, CodeMeta, and Zenodo JSON.
suggestions: Publish the synthetic generator scripts, converter wrappers, and raw outputs in a public repository to enable community verification.
Sample a collection of real-world CITATION.cff files from GitHub or Zenodo to measure how often these edge-case divergence patterns occur in practice.
Expand the differential evaluation beyond BibTeX and APA to include CodeMeta and Zenodo JSON.
